shadowDiff.ariaLabel: Ledger and derived path compared per turn
shadowDiff.title: Are the two ways of measuring a turn still agreeing?
shadowDiff.about: A watchdog, not a metric: it recomputes every TTFF and E2E figure the second way - from the paired message timestamps rather than the turn ledger - and compares them turn by turn. While it reads zero disagreements, the Performance figures are trustworthy for a reason you can point at. A row means the two have come apart, so treat those numbers as unsafe until it is understood.
shadowDiff.source: Every latency figure in the console comes from the turn ledger. This panel only checks it against the older derived path, and changes nothing.
shadowDiff.tolerance: Agree means every figure present on one side is present on the other and within {{ms}} ms. Both sides subtract the same instants, so the only expected difference is integer rounding; anything wider means the two picked different instants.
shadowDiff.exchangeAnchored: {{count}} of the turns both paths measured have no ledger user message, so the ledger TTFF starts from the exchange's user instant and that agreement shares its start with the derived path.
shadowDiff.loadFailed: The shadow diff failed to load.
shadowDiff.empty: No turn in this window was measured by both paths, so there is nothing to compare - which is not the same as agreement.
shadowDiff.allAgree: Every turn both paths measured agreed, and neither path measured a turn the other did not.
shadowDiff.truncated: Showing {{shown}} of {{total}} turns that need a look, largest difference first.
shadowDiff.filterEmpty: No turn in this window is in that class.

latency.title: Response latency
latency.aboutText: Each figure is averaged over the turns that recorded it. Multi-step task turns are left out unless you include them or choose a task type under Response type. Full definitions are in
latency.auroraOnly: These figures need Aurora mode. This deployment runs Athena, so the cards stay empty. Browser timings on the Client tab are not affected.
latency.notOptimized: Agent Echelon ships without some performance settings, to keep costs down. Production deployments should review them:
latency.description: Where a turn's time goes, from the message arriving to the finished answer.
latency.taskTurnHint: Multi-step task turns. Each turn is timed on its own, not the whole task.
latency.taskTurnsIncluded: Task turns included. Each is timed on its own, and the single-reply targets do not apply.
latency.taskTurnsExcluded_one: {{count}} multi-step task turn is left out, because one long step would hide how quickly ordinary replies arrive.
latency.taskTurnsExcluded_other: {{count}} multi-step task turns are left out, because one long step would hide how quickly ordinary replies arrive.
latency.ttffLead: TTFF is the time from a person sending a message to the assistant's placeholder appearing. Below is where that time goes. Router time is measured exactly, step by step, so it is the place to look first.
latency.ttffInferred: Turns where the send time had to be estimated are left out of this average.
latency.noPath_one: {{count}} turn has no recorded path and is in neither figure.
latency.noPath_other: {{count}} turns have no recorded path and are in neither figure.
latency.routerOverran: On average the router ran {{value}} longer than TTFF. It posts the placeholder partway through its work and keeps going, so its time overlaps TTFF instead of fitting inside it. The router steps below show where the time went.
latency.remainderMeasured: The last row is the message reaching the router plus the placeholder travelling back, measured per turn over {{count}} turns.
latency.remainderEstimated: The hatched row is an estimate: the difference between two averages over different turns. Use Inbound as an upper bound for it.
latency.counts: TTFF is averaged over {{ttff}} turns and Router over {{router}}. A step is recorded only on turns that ran it, so compare rows by their counts.
latency.coldStartCost_one: Cold starts add about {{value}} to TTFF, on the {{count}} turn that had one. The cost is spread across the rows above.
latency.coldStartCost_other: Cold starts add about {{value}} to TTFF, on the {{count}} turns that had one. The cost is spread across the rows above.
latency.overlapping: These cards overlap, so they do not add up. Classifier is part of Router, and Inbound covers both. Only the bars above split TTFF.
latency.reachingTheRouter: Reaching the router and the placeholder returning
latency.routerStepsLead: Each step the router took before handing the turn to the worker. A turn's steps add up to its Router time. Not every turn runs every step, so read the turn count beside each average.
latency.noRouterSteps: No router steps were recorded in this window.
latency.classifierSub: part of Router · {{coverage}} asked a model
latency.classifierNone: part of Router · no turn asked a model
latency.noColdStarts: no turn had a cold start
latency.workerLead: Worker compute is the time spent producing the answer after the placeholder is shown. None of it is inside TTFF, so do not add figures from the two sections together.
latency.p95SubFew: over {{count}} turns, too few for a reliable tail
latency.trendTitle: Worker compute against target, by day
latency.trendLead: Both lines are worker compute. P95 sits above the average because it follows the slowest turns. Watch for the two rising together.
latency.trendTargets: Dashed lines are targets; below is good.
latency.groupsLead: One row per day, assistant, delivery, path, role, profile version, classification and battle round, so two rows can share a date and assistant. Click a header to sort, or a row to see its turns.
latency.deliveryHelp: How the reply reached the person. Usually a placeholder that the final answer replaces.
latency.ttffColumnHelp: Message to placeholder. Blank where the reply was not paired with a message.
latency.noData: No latency data for this period.
latency.turnsError: Could not read the turns for this group.
latency.noClientTiming: The browser did not report a time for this turn.
latency.negativeGap: Negative: the browser and server clocks disagree on this turn.
latency.positiveGap: Network delivery and rendering in the browser.
latency.remainderSplit_one: On the {{count}} standard turn where the channel flow recorded when it received the message: reaching the flow {{toFlow}} (approximate, two clocks), the flow handing to the router {{flowToRouter}}, and the placeholder returning {{placeholderReturn}}.
latency.remainderSplit_other: On the {{count}} standard turns where the channel flow recorded when it received the message: reaching the flow {{toFlow}} (approximate, two clocks), the flow handing to the router {{flowToRouter}}, and the placeholder returning {{placeholderReturn}}.

ttff_ms.description: Time from a person sending a message to the assistant's placeholder appearing. Averaged over turns someone was waiting on. Good is under 1 second; over 2 seconds needs attention.
ttff_ms.label: First update (TTFF)

avg_total_ms.description: Time spent producing the answer after the placeholder is shown: loading history, calling the model and tools, and checking the reply. It leaves out the wait before the placeholder and posting the answer, so it is always less than E2E. Good is under 10 seconds.
avg_total_ms.label: Worker compute

avg_e2e_ms.description: Time from a person sending a message to the finished answer replacing the placeholder: the full wait. Good is under 10 seconds; past 30 seconds people give up.
avg_e2e_ms.label: E2E

p95_total_ms.description: The worker compute time that 95 of every 100 turns finish within, so it shows the slow turns an average hides. Good is under 15 seconds. Over fewer than about 20 turns it is close to the single slowest turn.
p95_total_ms.label: P95 worker compute

avg_bedrock_ms.description: Time spent in the model loop per turn: every model call plus the tools those calls ran. Usually the largest part of worker compute.
avg_bedrock_ms.label: Model loop

error_rate.description: Share of requests that ended in an error over the window. A reliability default. Tune the target to your own SLO.
error_rate.label: Error rate

reconnect_rate.description: WebSocket reconnects as a share of connections. A rising rate is usually the first sign of Chime instability or browser-tab WS suspension at scale.
reconnect_rate.label: WS reconnect rate

relevance_score.description: How well the answer addressed what was asked, scored 0 to 100 by an evaluation model that also reads the earlier turns. Averaged over judged turns. Good is 75 or higher; under 50 needs attention.
relevance_score.label: Relevance

intent_confidence.description: How sure the classifier was that it picked the right intent: high counts 100, medium 50 and low 0, averaged. Good is 80 or higher. A low score points to unclear intents, not bad answers.
intent_confidence.label: Routing confidence

task_completion_rate.description: Share of multi-step tasks that finished successfully. The rest are shown as failed, abandoned or still running. Good is 80% or higher.
task_completion_rate.label: Task completion

cost_per_reply.description: Model spend per reply in US dollars: the classifier plus every Converse call in the answer's tool loop, at each model's published price. Guardrails, evaluation and infrastructure are left out, so the real cost is higher by an amount this console does not measure. It is not your bill; use it to compare intents, and good is under one cent.
cost_per_reply.label: Model cost per reply

tool_error_rate.description: Share of tool calls that failed. Calls a task workflow refused by its own rules are counted as Refused, not as errors. Good is under 5%.
tool_error_rate.label: Tool errors

user_flag_rate.description: Share of rated replies that people marked "Needs work". Rating is optional, so unrated replies are not approval. Good is under 10%.
user_flag_rate.label: User signal

signup_conversion.description: Sessions that confirmed an account over sessions that viewed the sign-up form. An engagement default. Tune to your baseline.
signup_conversion.label: Signup conversion

signin_conversion.description: Sessions that signed in over sessions that viewed the sign-in form. A low value can indicate credential or auth-flow friction. A visit that never signs in sends no events, so it is not counted.
signin_conversion.label: Signin success

client_ttff_ms.label: TTFF in the browser
client_ttff_ms.description: The same wait as TTFF, timed by the person's browser from pressing send to the placeholder showing. The difference from TTFF is network delivery and rendering. A negative difference means the browser and server clocks disagree.

inbound_ms.label: Inbound
inbound_ms.description: Time from the message being sent to the worker starting, including the router, the classifier and any cold start. It overlaps Router and Classifier, so do not add them together. It compares two clocks, so it is approximate.

router_ms.label: Router
router_ms.description: Time the router spends on a turn, from receiving it to handing it to the worker: reading the conversation, choosing the assistant, classifying the intent and posting the placeholder.

classifier_ms.label: Classifier
classifier_ms.description: Time spent asking a model which intent a message is. Part of Router, not added to it. Averaged only over turns that asked a model.

cold_start_rate.label: Cold starts
cold_start_rate.description: Share of turns that ran on a newly started worker, which adds setup time. The worker records this itself. The card shows how much cold starts added to TTFF.

placeholder_resolve_ms.label: Answer target check
placeholder_resolve_ms.description: Time the worker spends confirming which chat message the answer replaces. Usually one quick read; it includes a conversation scan when one was needed.

guard_ms.label: Turn claim
guard_ms.description: Time the worker spends claiming the turn so it is answered only once, plus recording task status on task turns. Task turns read higher here.

poll_rate.label: Placeholder scan rate
poll_rate.description: Share of turns where the worker had to scan the conversation to find the placeholder because the router did not pass it on. Good is zero. Figures before 23 September 2026 count something else.

poll_ms.label: Placeholder scan cost
poll_ms.description: How long one scan took, on the turns that needed one. Read it beside the scan rate: a rare scan is still seconds for the person waiting.

model_ms.label: Model time
model_ms.description: Time spent waiting on model calls in the model loop, without the tools.

tool_ms.label: Tool time
tool_ms.description: Time spent running tools in the model loop, such as reading company documents. A turn that retrieves a lot shows here, not as slow model time.

tail_ms.label: Other worker time
tail_ms.description: Worker compute not covered by Turn claim, Answer target check or the model loop: mostly loading history and building the prompt. It is the remainder, so a negative value means time was counted against the wrong turn.

grounded_rate.label: Groundedness
grounded_rate.description: Share of answers fully supported by the passages the turn retrieved. Only turns that retrieved something are counted.

compliance_rate.label: Compliance
compliance_rate.description: Share of judged answers that broke none of this deployment's policy rules. A blocking breach is one the rules say must not reach a person.

flags_raised.label: Flags raised
flags_raised.description: Replies flagged on purpose with a reason, by a person, a moderator or the evaluation model. A flag is separate from a thumbs-down rating.

workflow_refusals.label: Refused
workflow_refusals.description: Times the model tried a task move its workflow does not allow, such as skipping a step or finishing without the document. The workflow refused and told the model why. A high count means the instructions and the workflow disagree.

platform_actions.label: Platform actions
platform_actions.description: Steps the platform ran for this intent without a model call, because a workflow step names a tool as its action. Not included in the tool count.

passages_used.label: Retrieved passages used
passages_used.description: Of the passages each turn retrieved, the share the answer relied on. A low share means retrieval brings back material the answer does not need.

volume.label: Volume
volume.description: Exchanges classified to this intent in the window. An exchange is one message and the assistant's reply.

flow_score.label: Flow score
flow_score.description: Overall quality of a multi-step task, scored 0 to 100 by an evaluation model: outcome 30%, information gathered 25%, and efficiency, context and experience 15% each. Good is 75 or higher.

e2e_p95_ms.label: P95
e2e_p95_ms.description: The end-to-end time that 95 of every 100 turns finish within. Cold starts and long tool loops show here first.

user_positive_rate.label: User ratings
user_positive_rate.description: Share of rated replies that people marked helpful. Rating is optional, so it describes the people who rated, not every reply.

unservedSubjects.title: Subjects no intent serves
unservedSubjects.about: General and off-topic turns, counted against the subjects of the conversation each happened in. A subject that keeps drawing them is a candidate for a new intent. A turn counts toward every subject of its conversation, so these counts rank subjects rather than adding up to a number of turns.
unservedSubjects.empty: No general or off-topic turns in this window.
unservedSubjects.failed: The subject breakdown could not be loaded.
unservedSubjects.unsupported: This view needs Aurora analytics mode.

turnKinds.title: Turn kinds
turnKinds.about: Not every message an assistant posts is an answer, and each kind explains itself on hover. Exchanges should be zero on every kind except Answer; a non-zero value there means something paired a turn that declared it was not answering.
turnKinds.empty: No assistant messages in this window.

help.answer: An ordinary reply to a message. The only kind the published response-time limits were written about, and the only one that mints an exchange.
help.reading: Queue work. A reading answers a BURST of messages rather than one of them, so there is no single message it could name and it never pairs.
help.drift: A suggestion that the conversation has moved on. It IS a response to a message and names it, but it deliberately does not do the work, so it is kept out of the population that measures answers.
help.welcome: What a conversation opens with. It fires on the assistant joining the channel, so it answers no message - pairing it would attach it to whatever happened to precede it and report a reply time measured from nothing.
help.notification: A message the platform sent that nobody asked for: a task assignment, a reminder, anything one-directional. Nobody was waiting on it, so it has no reply time and mints no exchange.
help.handover: A private message one assistant posted to hand a person's message to another assistant. Not an answer, so it never pairs; see Handovers for whether it was answered.
help.receipt: The placeholder of a turn whose answer was delivered as a message of its own, such as a private reply or an answer posted after a queue. It only points to where the answer went, so it never pairs; the answer pairs with the person's message.
help.queue_ack: A queue notice: the reply a message gets while the assistant is still busy with an earlier one, including a notice written into that earlier turn's placeholder. It acknowledges a wait rather than answering, so it never pairs.
help.join_recap: The catch-up a person is sent privately when they are added to a conversation. It answers the membership event that added them, not a message, so it never pairs; its time runs from that membership event to the recap.
help.event_step: An assistant turn an event workflow ran, such as the ops room's first look. Nobody asked a question it answers, so it never pairs; its time runs from the event that started the run to the post.
help.task_step: An assistant taking up a task assigned to it while nothing else was running in the conversation. Nobody asked a question it answers at that moment, so it never pairs; its time runs from when the task became ready to the post.
help.notice: A fixed message the platform posts as the assistant, such as a member joining or a refusal it states itself. Nobody asked a question it answers, so it never pairs.
help.battle-notice: A fixed message a battle posts, such as a round starting or a side being picked. It reports the battle rather than answering, so it never pairs.
help.fallback: A kind of turn this console has no description for yet.

turnKinds.theTurnKindBreakdownFailed: The turn-kind breakdown failed to load.
turnKinds.isThePopulationEveryResponse: is the population every response-time figure is about.
turnKinds.declareThatTheyAreSomething: declare that they are something else, and are counted here rather than being invisible.
turnKinds.isMeasuredFromTheMessage: is measured from the message each turn named, so a fast non-answer is visible without being averaged into the figures that measure answering.
turnKinds.ofSaidWhichMessageThey: {{v}} of {{messageCount}} said which message they were responding to. The rest are paired by inference, or not at all.
turnKinds.ofOrdinaryRepliesPairedInto: {{n}} of {{messageCount}} ordinary replies paired into an exchange. The gap is turns that answered nobody - a welcome, a continuation chunk - plus any that should have paired and did not.
turnKinds.measuredFromTheMessageEach: Measured from the message each turn NAMED, over {{replyMeasuredCount}} of {{messageCount}} turns. Not an exchange latency, and deliberately not mixed into one.
turnKinds.zeroWhichIsCorrectThis: Zero, which is correct: this kind declares that it is not an answer, so nothing should pair it as one.
turnKinds.nothingToMeasureFromThese: Nothing to measure from: these turns named no message, or the message they named is outside the window.
turnKinds.aTurnThatDeclaredIt: A turn that declared it is not an answer was paired as one. This is a defect in the pairing, not a property of the data.

handovers.title: Handovers
handovers.about: When an assistant recognizes that a person's message belongs to another assistant in the room, it posts a private handover to that assistant and tells the room where the question went. Sent counts those handovers. Answered counts the ones whose receiving assistant started its turn. Unanswered is the gap: handovers that were refused or never delivered. A handover is a message, so it is in message totals, and it appears in Turn kinds as its own kind.

experiments.addendumHelp: A tested instruction is added after the assistant's persona on every turn of that side, so one change is tested without writing a new persona. For example, to test whether shorter replies are rated higher, give B "Keep every reply under 80 words." and leave A blank. If B wins, promoting it carries the instruction to the live assistant, and Move into the persona on its draft makes it part of the persona's How to answer section. How the assistant answers in general belongs in the persona, not here.

On: battle turns are added to the averages, which biases the comparison because a battle variant is chosen, not assigned. People's picks are reported separately either way.
experiments.aboutText: An experiment splits one classification's traffic between variants and compares quality, task completion, latency and cost. A classification runs one experiment at a time. Battle turns are left out of the comparison by default, because a battle variant is chosen rather than randomly assigned; people's picks are reported separately.
experiments.description: Which variant should ship, decided from its own traffic.
experiments.imageVariantsHelp: Each variant uses a different image model. Ordinary traffic gets the assigned variant's model, and a battle runs both and scores them. Text turns and battle rebuttals use the profile's normal model.
experiments.battleOptionHelp: Battle is an option on this experiment, not a separate path. Both variants answer every /battle prompt the way ordinary requests are answered, with the same intents, models and tools. In round 1 both answer at once; in round 2 each replies briefly to the other, and a scorecard closes the battle. It stays on until an admin or the experiment owner turns it off, and conversation moderators choose which conversations take part.

create.title: Create an assistant
create.intro: Two steps make the assistant: its classification, role and name, then its starting point and models. The assistant is built in the background with a first draft, and the next steps edit that draft in the sections the assistant's page uses: Behavioral, Workflows, Scope and models, and Tools and context. The last step validates the draft and activates it.

messageTemplates.title: Message templates
messageTemplates.help: Everything this assistant says for a platform event is edited here: every line it posts or emails, and the request its join recap answers, is a template. Each message is said from the shipped template, the classification's, or one of this assistant's own. With no choice in this version, the first that exists is used: this assistant's own, then the classification's, then the shipped one. Saving this assistant's own template makes it available at once; it is not part of a version. Which template this version uses is picked under Used in this version, and saved with the draft.

A written variant is always said as written. If the call fails, is blocked, runs late, runs long or adds a figure, a link or a handle the text does not have, the written text is posted instead. Each call is counted against the deployment's budget.

welcome.builtIn: With Opening text blank, the opening is put together from what the conversation and the deployment carry, each part left out when there is nothing for it: a greeting naming the company, why this conversation exists (its topic, the event that opened it, or the conversation it continues), what the person's access covers, "A few things you can try:" with your suggested prompts, and a closing note. The company, the access line and the closing note are set once for the whole deployment. With none of these, it says: "Hi - I'm your assistant for this conversation. I can answer questions, draft documents, analyse data, help with code, or work through a plan with you. What would you like to start with?"

A line that names a field the conversation does not have is dropped, so put each conditional sentence on a line of its own. To say something different in a different kind of conversation, give that conversation type its own opening text.

The last three belong to the conversation, so they count for every assistant the person spoke with there. Two people's signals are never added together.

retrievalSources.title: Retrieval by source
retrievalSources.tip: For each context source, how often retrieval brought back a passage from it and how often the answer rested on one, as the groundedness judge reported. A source retrieved often and used rarely is for whoever curates it to fix. Whether the right passages were retrieved at all is not measured here.

retrievalSources.error: Could not load retrieval by source.

judgeCalibration.title: How far each judge agrees with people
judgeCalibration.tip: Each judge compared with people's labels on the same answers. Kappa is agreement after removing what chance alone would give: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than chance. Caught is the share of failures people found that the judge also found; passed is the share of good answers it also passed. People is how far two people agree on the same answers, which is about the best a judge can be expected to match. A new judge model or rubric version is a new row.

judgeCalibration.selfJudged: {{count}} of {{judged}} of {{assistant}}'s answers were judged by {{model}}, the model that wrote them.

toolOutcomes.title: Tool use
toolOutcomes.tip: Each tool call scored by what it did. A failed call is read from the error the turn recorded, and a call that changes something from the platform's record of the change; the judge decides the rest. Errors and empty results are for the tool's owner to fix; wrong arguments, a reply the result does not support, and a tool left unused are for the assistant's team.

workflowEditor.title: This version's event workflows
workflowEditor.help: A workflow runs on the event it names: the assistant joining (assistant-joined), an event opening a conversation of a type it lists (conversation-opened), a person joining (person-joined), an invitation sent or still unredeemed at its deadline, or the alarm an ops room watches changing state (alarm-state-changed). Steps run from the top: a send posts a message template, an assistant step answers from a prompt template with read tools, a deadline and a fallback, an onboarding intake asks the intake questions, and an end step finishes the run. A welcome names its assistant-joined or conversation-opened workflow; every other event runs the one workflow this version declares on it. A person-joined workflow is followed by the join recap unless it writes its own.

A person is told privately and by email, and answers in the conversation or on the task's card. The run goes on when the task ends: Then for a finished task, If it fails for any other ending, and If the deadline passes when nobody finished it.
workflowEditor.intakeHelp: Asks this assistant's intake questions with no model call, privately, to the one person the event names. A person already onboarded, or with nothing left to ask, is asked nothing and the run goes on. Only one person's intake runs in a conversation at a time.

A participant role names its holders who are members, as a list, from the roles the conversation's type declares.

variables.pickDecide: Add a condition on a variable
variables.help: Every value this assistant may read: the variables its version names, then every source its classification publishes. Each says its type and its trust. Platform, operator and closed-list values may decide; text a person or an outside system wrote is inserted, never decides.
variables.unreadable: The classification's sources could not be read, so only the sources every classification publishes are listed.

refused.member: Member text never decides: a person or an outside system wrote it.
refused.person: A fact about one person, so it reaches only a message addressed to that person, never one the room reads.
refused.mentionOnly: The room may read a display name only as a mention, which a workflow send binds.
refused.nameFirst: Name it as a variable of this version first (variables, edited as JSON with a draft patch), then insert it by that name.

messageChoices.title: Used in this version
messageChoices.help: Which template this version says the message from: the shipped one, the classification's, or one of this assistant's own. With conditions, the first alternative whose condition holds is said, else the last. Saved with the draft as messages, and checked when the draft is validated.
messageChoices.orderOption: No choice: this assistant's own, else the classification's, else the shipped one
messageChoices.classificationNoneOption: The classification's template (it has none, so the shipped one)
messageChoices.readByRoom: The room reads this message, so a fact about one person cannot choose it.
messageChoices.readOnly: Changing which template this version uses needs the edit-profiles capability.

routingRules.title: Routing rules
routingRules.help: The first rule whose condition holds serves the turn on its model, after an experiment and before the built-in context rules. Only the models this assistant's classification selects are offered, and a condition is read as the room reads the reply, so no fact about one person routes a turn.

help.identity: The name people see beside the assistant's messages and type after @, and the persona the assistant answers with. Activating a new name renames the messaging identity too.
help.abilities: The tools the assistant is offered, the guardrail on every reply, and the context sources read into each turn. The classification decides what a tool may reach; this list decides what the assistant is offered.
help.models: The model that writes the answers, the one that classifies each message, and a model per intent, from the models the classification selects.
help.routing: Rules checked in order before the intent routes: the first whose condition holds serves the turn on its model.
help.welcome: What the assistant says when added to a conversation: the welcome workflow WelcomeIntent starts, per kind of conversation. The opening is a template, a prompt turn may follow, and a welcome that continues is edited under Event workflows.
help.messages: The lines the assistant posts for platform events, each a template. A saved template is in use at once; which template each message uses is part of the draft.
help.events: Workflows an event starts: someone joining, an invitation, a deadline, an alarm. The welcome is the one on assistant-joined.
help.variables: Named values the templates and conditions read, each a source and a fallback. Variables are edited as JSON, and this step says how.

discard.title: Discard this draft?
discard.lostAll: Everything in the draft is lost. Nothing is active yet, so Start first draft begins again from the classification's defaults.
discard.lostNothing: The draft matches the active version, so no change is lost.
discard.servingUnchanged: The active version keeps serving, and Edit starts a fresh draft from the active version.
discard.done: The draft was discarded. Nothing serving changed.
discard.changed: The draft was not discarded: it was saved again after this page loaded it. The newer draft is shown now; discard it again if it should go.
discard.gone: There was no draft to discard; it was already activated or discarded elsewhere.

draftCards.diffNone: Nothing differs from the active version.

goldenUpload.title: Add golden entries
goldenUpload.tip: Cases beside the answers people labeled: your own, uploaded from a file, or written from what each intent of the draft says it covers. Each enters as a capability entry; once the active version passes it in a run, it can be promoted to regression.
goldenUpload.help: A JSON Lines file (one entry per line) or a CSV file with a header row. Columns: intent and request, and optionally reference, precedingTurns (a JSON list of {"role", "text"}) and replyPreferences (a JSON object of reply-preference keys). Up to 100 entries, the most the set holds, and 1 MB. Personal details are removed before anything is stored.
goldenUpload.done: Added {{count}} entries to the golden set as capability entries.

problemCode.UNKNOWN_FIELD: "{{field}}" is not a column of an upload
problemCode.UNKNOWN_INTENT: the intent is not one of this assistant's pack
problemCode.BAD_TURNS: precedingTurns must be up to six turns of {"role": "user" or "assistant", "text"}
problemCode.UNKNOWN_PREFERENCE: replyPreferences names a key or value the preference registry does not declare
problemCode.WRONG_CELL_COUNT: the row has a different number of cells than the header
problemCode.DUPLICATE: the same request for the same intent appears earlier in the file

refusal.TOO_LARGE: The file is {{bytes}} bytes; an upload is at most {{max}}.
refusal.TOO_MANY_LINES: The file holds {{lines}} entries; an upload is at most {{max}}.
refusal.BAD_HEADER: The CSV header must name columns from: {{columns}}, with intent and request, each once. It names: {{found}}.
refusal.INVALID_LINES: {{count}} of {{lines}} lines are not entries, so nothing was stored. Correct them and upload the file again.
refusal.GOLDEN_SET_FULL: The set holds {{live}} live entries; adding {{adding}} would pass the {{capacity}} a run can answer. Retire some first.
refusal.DETECTOR_UNAVAILABLE: This deployment has no detector to remove personal details with, so nothing was stored.
refusal.DETECTOR_FAILED: Personal details could not be checked in {{count}} lines, so nothing was stored.
refusal.GOLDEN_RUN_UNAVAILABLE: This deployment keeps no golden set (it is kept in Aurora mode only).
refusal.GENERATION_FAILED: The model wrote nothing usable for {{count}} intents ({{intents}}), so nothing was stored. If it happens again, the cause is in the golden run function's log.
refusal.UNKNOWN_INTENT: These are not intents of the draft: {{intents}}.
refusal.TOO_MANY_INTENTS: One generation covers at most {{max}} named intents.
refusal.BAD_PER_INTENT: Choose from 1 to {{max}} requests per intent.
refusal.DETECTOR_BUSY: The service that removes personal details was too busy, so nothing was stored. Send the file again in a few minutes.
refusal.BATCH_FAILED: It did not finish, so nothing was stored: {{error}}
refusal.NO_INTENTS: The draft's pack declares no intents to write requests for.

goldenUpload.generateHelp: Or write requests for the draft's intents from what each intent says it covers, starting with the intents the set covers least (at most 12 at a time). One model call per intent. They are marked generated and refuse nothing until the active version passes them and someone promotes them.
